summary: Describes an experiment in using the DNS to carry routing information, as a possible way to ease the routing table explosion. It defines an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary:
Every network that connects to the Internet has to be listed in the routing tables of the networks in the middle. As more and more networks do this, those tables grow.

This RFC suggests putting the list in the DNS instead. A router that does not know where to send a packet looks the destination up in the DNS, gets back the addresses of the gateways that lead there, and picks one.

subtitle: An experiment in letting the DNS say which gateway a remote network should be reached through.

tldr.problem: The routing tables of the Internet's transit networks grow with every network that announces itself, which makes routers bigger, route exchanges heavier and administration slower.
tldr.mechanism: The scheme adds an MX-like record, called an RX record, to the DNS holding the addresses of the gateways that lead to a network, each with a preference value. A router that cannot find a route asks the DNS, picks a gateway from the records, and sends the packet with a source route through it.
tldr.outcome: All the routing decisions are made once, at or near the source, which keeps the transit routers unchanged. The code was under development at INRIA and was to be placed in the public domain.

today: RFC 1383 is an Experimental document from December 1992 and has not been obsoleted. It proposes an experiment in directory-based routing; the code was under development at INRIA and was to be placed in the public domain.

sections.title: The Routing Explosion Problem
sections.content:
Several recent studies had outlined the risk of routing explosion in the current Internet: there were already more than 5000 networks announced in the NSFNET routing tables and more than 7000 in the EBONE routing tables. As these numbers grow, several problems occur. The size of the routing tables grows linearly with the number of connected networks, and handling larger tables requires more resources in all intelligent routers, in particular in all transit and external routers that cannot rely on default routes. The volume of information carried by route exchange protocols such as BGP grows with the number of networks, using more network resources and making the reaction to routing events slower. And explicit administrative decisions have to be exercised by all transit network administrators who want to implement routing policies for each and every additional multi-homed network.

The current textbook solution to the routing explosion problem is hierarchical routing based on hierarchical addresses. This is largely documented in routing protocols such as IDRP, and is one of the rationales for deploying the CIDR addressing structure in the Internet. The textbook solution, while often perfectly adequate, has a number of inconveniences, particularly in the presence of multihomed stubs, such as customer networks that are connected to more than one service provider.

The scheme in this memo allows for simple routing. It is complementary with the classic hierarchical routing approach, but provides an easy to implement and low cost solution for multi-homed domains. The solution is a generalization of the MX record scheme currently used for mail routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Transit networks have to hold an entry for every network that reaches them through it, and that list is getting long. The usual fix, grouping addresses into blocks, does not suit a customer who buys service from two providers at once.

sections.title: Routing Based on RX Records
sections.content:
MX records are currently used by the mail routing application to introduce a level of decoupling between the domain names used for user registration and the mailbox addresses. They are particularly useful for sending mail to non-connected domains, where the MX record points to one or several Internet hosts that accept to relay mail towards the target domain.

This scheme generalizes that for packet routing. Suppose a routing domain D, containing several networks, subnetworks and hosts, connected to the Internet through a couple of IP gateways. These gateways are dual homed: each has an address within the domain D, say D1 and D2, and an address within the Internet, say I1 and I2. These gateways also have a particularity: they retain information and do not try to announce to the Internet any reachability information on the networks contained within D. Those networks have nevertheless been properly registered: a name server accessible from the Internet holds the in-addr.arpa records that enable reverse address-to-name lookup, and also holds the network level equivalent of MX records, say RX records. Given any host address Dx within D, one can get RX records pointing to the Internet addresses of the gateways, I1 and I2.

A standard Internet router cannot in principle send a packet to the address Dx, because it has no corresponding routing information. If it has been modified to exploit the scheme, it will query the DNS with the name built up from Dx in the in-addr.arpa domain, obtain the RX records, and forward the packet towards I1 or I2 using some form of source routing. The gateway I1 or I2 receives the packet, its routing tables contain information on the domain D, and it can relay the packet to the host Dx.

The scheme avoids changes in host IP addresses as topology changes, without requiring extra overhead on routing, provided that the routing employs some form of hierarchical information aggregation or abstraction. It also allows multi-homed domains to be supported without additional overhead on routing and without requiring hosts to have explicit knowledge of multiple addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The domain does not announce its internal networks to the rest of the Internet. Instead it registers, in the DNS, the addresses of the gateways that lead into it. A router that cannot find a route asks the DNS and is told which gateway to use.

sections.title: Choosing a Gateway
sections.content:
Allowing only one RX record per destination would guarantee consistent decisions in the network, but it has a number of draw-backs: a single access point would be a single point of failure, and it would be connected to only one transit network, keeping the customer locking effect of hierarchical routing.

The proposal is that the RX records have a structure parallel to that of MX records, carrying with each gateway address a preference identifier. The source host, when making the routing decision based on RX records, should list all possible gateways, prune all gateways in the list which are known to be unreachable from the local site, and, if the local host is present in the list with a preference index x, prune all gateways whose preference index is larger than x or equal to x. It then chooses one of the gateways in the list; if the list is empty, the destination is considered unreachable. These evaluations should not be repeated for every packet: the routers should maintain a cache of the most frequently used destinations.

In theory one could extract distance information from the local routing table and combine it with the preference index to choose the best gateway. In practice, as shown in the mail context, it is extremely difficult to perform this kind of test, and one has to rely on more heuristic approaches. The easiest is always to choose the preferred gateway, the one with the minimal preference index. Alternatively one could choose a gateway at random within the list, which would spread traffic over several routes and is known to introduce better load sharing and more redundancy.

Because the decision is made only once, the particular algorithm to use can be left as a purely local matter: one domain may base it purely on the RX record, another purely on the routing information to the gateways listed in the RX record, and a third may use weighted combinations of both.

The most important feature, the RFC says, is the ability to cope rapidly with network errors, that is, to detect that one of the routes has become unreachable. Possible solutions include letting intermediate gateways rewrite the loose source route to replace an unreachable access point by a better alternative, monitoring the LSR options in incoming packets and using the reverse LSR, monitoring the ICMP Unreachable messages received from intermediate gateways, and regularly probing the LSR to check that it is still useful.
sections.plainLanguage: Several gateways may be listed for one destination, each with a preference number. The sender drops the ones it knows are broken, drops any worse than its own preference, and picks one of the rest.

sections.title: Connectivity and the Way Back
sections.content:
A scheme relying on RX records is only valid if these records can be accessed. By definition, this is not the case of the target domain itself, which is located at the outer fringes of the Internet. A domain that wants to obtain connectivity using the RX scheme will have to replicate its domain name service information, and in particular the RX records, so it has to provide them through servers accessible from the core of the Internet. A very obvious way to do this is to locate replicated name servers for the target domain in the access gateways I1 and I2.

A source located in the fringe domain, when accessing a core Internet host, will have to choose an access relay. A first approach is to let the access gateway relay the general routing information provided by the routing domains through the fringe network, so that the fringe hosts have the same connectivity as the core hosts and do not have to use source directed routing. This leaves the packets untouched, but may pose problems should the transit network need to send back an ICMP packet, which would then have to specify a source route through the access gateway. That would be guaranteed if the IP packets are source routed, as the reverse source route would be used automatically for the ICMP packet, so the RFC recommends that all IP packets leaving a fringe domain be explicitly source routed.

The source route could be inserted by the access gateway when the packet exits the fringe domain, if the gateway has been made aware of the scheme. It can also be set by the source host, which would then have to explicitly choose the transit gateway, or by the first router in the path, usually the default router of the host sending the packets. As the RFC expects hosts to be easier to modify than routers, it develops the algorithms for the host case. The fringe hosts have to know the set of available gateways, of which all temporarily unreachable gateways shall be pruned, and in the absence of more information the gateway will be chosen according to some preference order, or possibly at random. If a fringe host wants to communicate with another fringe host, it will have to insert two relays in the source route, one for the domain that sources the packet and one for the domain where the destination resides.

The memo assumes that all gateways to a fringe domain are equivalent, since the objective of the experiment is to test a simple form of directory based routing rather than to provide a particular policy routing solution. Some form of policy routing could however be implemented as a simple extension: RX records are only qualified by an order of preference, and it would not be difficult to also qualify them with a supported policy indication, such as the numeric identifier of a particular policy. When going towards a fringe network one should prune from the usable list all the gateways that do not support at least one of the local policies; when exiting a fringe network one should assess the policies supported by the target and pick a corresponding exit gateway; and when going from one fringe network to another one should pick a pair of exit and access gateway that have matching policies.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme has a catch: the DNS records for a fringe domain have to be reachable from the core of the Internet, so the domain must run copies of its name service inside its gateways. Traffic coming back the other way needs an explicit source route, so that error messages find their way home.

sections.title: The Experimental Software
sections.content:
The experimental software, implemented under BSD Unix in a socket environment, contains two tasks: a real time forwarder, implemented inside the kernel, which handles the source demanded routes, and a DNS query manager, which transmits to the real time forwarder the source routing information.

In a definitive scheme it would be necessary to define a DNS record type and the corresponding RX format, and to teach the new format to the domain name service software. While not very difficult to do, that would probably take a couple of months and is not used in the early experimentations, which use the general purpose TXT record. That record is designed for easy general purpose extensions in the DNS and its content is a text string.

The RX record contains three fields: a record identifier composed of the two characters RX, used to disambiguate from other experimental uses of the TXT record; a cost indicator encoded on up to three numerical digits, whose corresponding positive integer value should be less than 256 in order to preserve future evolutions; and an IP address encoded as a text string in dot notation. The three strings are separated by a single comma. The example given is a TXT record for the domain *.27.32.192.in-addr.arpa with the value RX, 10, 10.0.0.7, which means that for all hosts whose IP address starts by the three octets 192.32.27 the IP host 10.0.0.7 can be used as a gateway, and that the preference value is 10.

The real time forwarder sits alongside a standard IP router, as if it were a particular subnetwork connection: the IP router is told that some destinations should be forwarded to a particular interface, that is, through the real time forwarder. It is particularly important to know efficiently which destinations should be routed through the service, and since the service would be useless for destinations which are directly reachable, the implementation monitors the unreachable destinations by watching the ICMP messages that signal unreachable destination networks and copying them to the DNS query manager. For fringe networks, where the router knows that destinations outside the local domain will have to be routed through the real time forwarder, it makes sense to declare the real time forwarder as the default route for the host.

On receiving the ICMP message, the query manager updates the local routing table so that any new packet bound to the requested destination is routed through the real time forwarder. At the same time it sends a DNS request to read the RX records corresponding to the destination, and after the response it selects a gateway and passes the information to the real time forwarder.

When the real time forwarder receives a packet, it checks whether a gateway is known for the destination. If so, it looks at the packet, inserts the necessary source routing information, and forwards the packet either by resending it through the general IP routing program or by forwarding it directly to the network interface associated to the intermediate gateway. If the gateway is not yet known, the packet is placed in a waiting queue. Each time the query manager passes new gateway information, the queue is processed and the packets for which information has become available are forwarded. Packets in the waiting queue age: their time to live is decremented at regular intervals, and if it becomes null the packets are destroyed, and an ICMP message may be forwarded. If the query manager cannot find RX information for a destination, it signals to the real time forwarder that the destination is unreachable; the information is kept in the destination table, queued packets for that destination are destroyed, and new packets are not forwarded. The information in the destination table is not permanent: a time to live is associated with each line and the aging lines are periodically removed.
sections.plainLanguage: The experiment ran as two pieces of software on a Unix host: one that asks the DNS and picks a gateway, and one that sits beside the normal router and rewrites packets to go through that gateway.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section of RFC 1383 says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.

The scheme does rely on the DNS being trustworthy in one particular way. The RFC notes that a scheme relying on RX records is only valid if these records can be accessed, and that a domain wanting connectivity through the RX scheme has to replicate its domain name service information, and in particular the RX records, through servers accessible from the core of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: This document has almost nothing to say about security. Its security section says only that security issues are not discussed here.

viz.caption: How a gateway is chosen from the RX records (RFC 1383, Section 3.4)

items.title: List the gateways
items.text: Take all the possible gateways named in the RX records for the destination.

items.title: Prune the unreachable ones
items.text: Drop every gateway known to be unreachable from the local site.

items.title: Apply the local preference
items.text: If the local host is in the list with a preference index x, drop every gateway whose index is larger than x or equal to x.

items.title: Choose one
items.text: Pick one of the remaining gateways. If the list is empty, the destination is unreachable.
